query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid homogenization annealing treatment applied to the as‐fabricated nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will eliminate the incipient Cr/V segregation that seeds radiation‐induced precipitation, thereby preventing precipitate formation under 8 dpa energetic-particle irradiation while preserving the alloy's negligible irradiation hardening and rendering it more suitable for bulk fabrication.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced (e.g., via magnetron sputtering) that exhibits grain boundary segregation of Cr and V, which under irradiation leads to the formation of Cr/V-rich precipitates with minimal irradiation hardening.
generation.intervention: Introduce a single-step, rapid high-temperature homogenization annealing treatment designed to dissolve Cr/V segregation and achieve a uniform single-phase solid solution prior to bulk consolidation.
generation.conditions: The annealing should be performed at a controlled temperature (set below the onset of irradiation-induced phase instability) for a sufficient duration to homogenize element distribution, followed by consolidation into bulk form. Subsequent testing involves energetic-particle irradiation at a reactor-relevant temperature (e.g., ~1073 K) to a damage level of approximately 8 dpa.
generation.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous elemental distribution with reduced solute segregation at grain boundaries and triple junctions.
generation.mechanism: By dissolving the local Cr and V enrichments that act as nucleation sites for precipitate formation, the homogenization treatment prevents radiation-induced segregation from progressing to detectable second-phase precipitation. At the same time, maintaining a uniform microstructure preserves the inherent defect sink characteristics that yield negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified (as-deposited) alloy, the homogenized bulk alloy will exhibit little to no radiation-induced Cr/V precipitation after exposure to 8 dpa, while retaining its near-constant hardness.
generation.baseline: The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy shows Cr/V-rich precipitates after irradiation at ~8 dpa, even though its overall irradiation hardening remains minimal.
generation.boundary: Irradiation performed at reactor-relevant temperatures (near 1073 K) up to 8 dpa; the annealing treatment must be chosen to homogenize the alloy without causing detrimental grain growth, thereby keeping within the thermal stability limits of the material.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature and duration to achieve full homogenization without coarsening remain to be precisely determined, and scale-up from thin-film/nanocrystalline samples to bulk consolidation may introduce additional variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloys: one set that undergoes the rapid homogenization anneal and a control set that remains in the as-deposited nanocrystalline state. Subject both sets to energetic-particle irradiation at a reactor-relevant temperature (e.g., ~1073 K) to a total damage of approximately 8 dpa.
measurements: Atom probe tomography (APT) to assess Cr and V distribution and detect any precipitate formation
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to observe microstructural features and defect structures
Nanoindentation to measure any changes in hardness post-irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (homogenized) alloy exhibits a level of radiation-induced Cr/V precipitation comparable to the unmodified control, or if irradiation hardening increases significantly relative to the baseline, then the intervention does not prevent the precipitation and the hypothesis is falsified.

() combined experiments and modeling to identify the sluggish mobility of dislocation loops as the main mechanism leading to radiation tolerance in Ni-based FCC HEAs. Kumar et al. () showed how Ni-based FCC HEAs lead to less radiation-induced segregation and fewer voids, although hardness was observed to increase after irradiation. Other studies show results in the same direction, with HEAs improving radiation tolerance in both FCC and BCC structures (). Very recently, W-based quinary HEAs with diverse composition have been synthesized as potential materials for fusion applications. The authors observed the formation of Ti carbides and laves phases at large W concentrations. The authors studied the mechanical response, showing that these materials could lead to twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening (). However, refractory HEAs have never been tested under irradiation for potential uses as PFMs or structural materials in nuclear fusion environments. The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
